name: registry
intent: Provide one well-known object through which otherwise unrelated objects register themselves and find one another by key, so callers can reach objects and services without holding a direct reference or knowing which concrete implementation is installed.
problem: Collaborating objects have no association to navigate along: the caller holds only an identifier - a name, a symbol, a type, a token - while the reference to the implementation that provides the behaviour is not available at that point in the code. Hard-coding the implementation or its construction at each call site couples every caller to one choice and scatters wiring decisions across the codebase, and the set of available implementations is not known at compile time (plug-ins, drivers, per-deployment services).
context: Applies inside one process or a well-scoped subsystem when several modules, services or plug-ins coexist and the set varies with configuration, packaging or plug-in availability - registration happening at start-up, at import/link time or through discovery, and lookup happening later from code that could not be handed a reference. Typical settings: service discovery inside an application container, plug-in/extension registries resolved by name, keyed factories for runtime identifiers (formats, protocols, message types) and shared subsystems (loggers, codecs, connection factories) that many parts must reach. It matters most where a framework owns object creation but clients still need a way to reach what was created.
benefits: Clients depend on a key and an interface instead of a concrete implementation or a constructor call: the implementation can be swapped, decorated or reconfigured without touching call sites.
One authoritative place to look: discovery, duplicate detection, listing ("what is available?") and lookup policy are implemented once in the registry instead of being re-invented at every use site.
Extensibility by addition: new services or plug-ins register themselves, so the code that consumes them does not change (open/closed principle), which is what makes plug-in ecosystems possible.
Decoupling from construction: the registry can own, cache or lazily create entries, so callers stay ignorant of creation cost, lifetime and configuration details.
Uniform lifecycle policy in one place - lazy versus eager, one instance per key, reset for tests - instead of scattered ad hoc singletons and caches.
A test seam: tests can populate the registry with doubles or install a fresh registry instead of exercising the real collaborators.
tradeoffs: Global mutable state: the registry is reachable from everywhere, so dependencies become ambient rather than visible in signatures - a component's API no longer reveals what it needs, which is exactly the Service Locator critique Fowler levelled against registry-style wiring.

Test isolation suffers: registrations outlive the test that created them, so suites need explicit teardown and start failing by order (database/sql ships an unexported unregisterAllDrivers for precisely this reason, and Rails registries must be cleared on code reload).

Lifetime and ordering hazards: entries are strongly referenced for the process lifetime unless removed, and the registry's own initialization may race with registrants (static initialization order, module load order, link-time inclusion) - a classic source of 'works sometimes' failures.

Concurrency: register and lookup must be made thread-safe (locks, concurrent maps) or restricted to single-threaded start-up; an unsynchronized global map is a data race waiting for the first late registration.

Failures arrive late and ambiguously: a missing key throws at lookup time far from the misconfiguration, and duplicate-registration semantics vary (panic, last-wins, silently ignored) so mistakes hide instead of surfacing.

A well-known object is a coupling magnet: everything reaches everything, module boundaries erode and the dependency graph becomes invisible; it is also strictly in-process - reaching services in another process or host is service discovery, a different mechanism.
Performance: a single locked table is a shared point of contention, so hot lookups need caching, read-mostly structures or per-consumer resolution.

participants.responsibility: The well-known object that owns the key-to-entry mapping and exposes the register and lookup operations; it defines the key type and the policy for duplicates, lifetimes and concurrency.

The identifier used to find an entry - a name, symbol, class/type, token or enum value. Keys are the registry's public contract, so their type, uniqueness and spelling rules matter as much as the stored values.
The object, service or factory entered into the registry and later resolved by clients; it is normally registered as a factory or supplier so creation stays lazy and lifetime stays with the registry.
The code that populates the registry - start-up wiring, a boot module, a plug-in loader, a discovery pass, or the registrant itself through self-registration.
Code that resolves entries by key and uses them through the interface, without holding a direct reference to the implementation or knowing how it was created.

use_cases: Plug-in and extension registries: a host resolves codecs, exporters, parsers, authentication mechanisms, world generators or rules by name, and third-party packages add their own registrations (Java SPI, Python entry points, Eclipse extension registry, database/sql drivers, mod loaders).

Service discovery inside an application container: framework and library services are registered under types or tokens at start-up and resolved by code that cannot receive them through constructors (framework callbacks, legacy helpers, static entry points).

Keyed factories: mapping an identifier that only arrives at runtime (protocol name, file format, message type, job kind) to the factory that builds the handler for it, keeping the dispatch table out of the caller.
Shared subsystems that must be reachable from many places without threading a reference through every layer: logger, metrics, configuration, connection factory, serializer.
Cross-package discovery where the provider must not be a compile-time dependency of the consumer: JARs on the class path, installed Python distributions, loadable modules or shared libraries.
Java's JDK ServiceLoader: a host discovers providers for a service interface from modules or META-INF/services and uses the common contract without compiling against each provider.
Python packaging entry points: installed distributions advertise named plug-in components in metadata, and consumers discover and load a selected group through importlib.metadata.
Eclipse Platform's extension registry: plug-ins declare extension points and contributions in plugin.xml, then the host queries Platform.getExtensionRegistry() to enumerate them.
avoid_when: The dependency can simply be handed over (constructor, setter, parameter or framework injection): a direct reference is more explicit, easier to test and cheaper at runtime - prefer dependency injection.
The set of collaborators is small and fixed: a plain field, a factory function or a switch over a closed enum is clearer than a global lookup.
The lookup would happen inside a library: libraries must not impose global state on their host - take the dependency or an explicit registry instance as a parameter.
The lookup crosses process or machine boundaries: what is needed there is service discovery (DNS, service mesh, distributed registry) or a message channel, not an in-process well-known object.
The only motive is avoiding plumbing a parameter through intermediate layers: that is a design smell, not a use case - shorten the path or introduce an explicit boundary instead.
anti_patterns: Service Locator: the registry used inside business code as a hidden dependency resolver, so every class silently reaches into global state instead of declaring what it needs, and tests must reset the world before running.
God registry: one process-wide map for every unrelated concern (configuration, services, domain objects, feature flags), coupling every module to every other through shared keys.
Silent overwrite: 'last registration wins' without duplicate detection, so the effective implementation depends on load order and configuration mistakes mask each other.
Registry as accumulation point: instances are registered and never removed, so the process holds every object it ever created and memory grows monotonically.
Type-erasure theatre: a stringly-typed registry whose lookups assert types with unchecked casts, presenting runtime failures as if they were type safety.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: clients depend on a key plus an abstract interface, and concrete implementations are supplied by wiring rather than chosen at the call site.
Open/closed principle: new implementations arrive by registering, not by editing the code that resolves them.
Separation of configuration from use: choosing and assembling implementations is a start-up concern; calling them is a runtime concern.
Information hiding: the registry owns its table and all policy (keys, duplicates, lifetimes, concurrency); clients see only lookup.
Single responsibility per participant: registration, resolution and entry lifecycle each have one home instead of being spread across call sites.
best_practices: Keep the registry to one narrow key domain and a typed interface; do not grow it into a general-purpose service bag.
Register factories or suppliers by default, instances only when the entry is genuinely shared, so creation and lifetime stay under the registry's policy.
Make duplicate handling explicit and fail fast (reject duplicates; provide a deliberate Replace/TryAdd operation when overwriting is legitimate).
Key by the most specific thing available - token, type, symbol or enum - rather than free-form strings, and validate keys at registration time.
Make the registry injectable and resettable so tests can install a fresh one and no state leaks between tests.
Define thread-safety for registration and lookup, and document whether registration is allowed after start-up.
Log registrations and support enumeration for diagnostics; bound growth with explicit removal, weak references or per-scope registries where entries are transient.
sources: Fowler, M., Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002), Base Patterns chapter - Registry (How It Works p. 480, When to Use It p. 482, Example: A Singleton Registry p. 483, Example: Thread-Safe Registry p. 484).
